title: Using Bulk Copy API for faster ingestion in Fabric Data Warehouse
summary: A Fabric Data Warehouse team post explaining when to use the preview Bulk Copy (BCP) API for client-side ingestion instead of the standard server-side COPY INTO path, with concrete usage patterns for application developers (SqlBulkCopy/SQLServerBulkCopy), script-driven operators (bcp.exe), and data-integration tool users (SSIS, Azure Data Factory, Informatica).
audience: Application developers, DBAs/SQL engineers running operational scripts, and data-integration engineers who need to write data into Fabric Data Warehouse directly from client code or tools rather than from staged files.
why_it_matters: It draws a clear boundary between two ingestion paths that are easy to conflate: COPY INTO for file-based, staged, server-side loading, versus BCP API for client-side application or tool-driven ingestion where staging isn't possible; picking the wrong one has real throughput and architectural consequences.
takeaways: BCP API is positioned as a client-side ingestion path for data produced in application code, not as a replacement for the recommended server-side COPY INTO staged-file loading pattern.
COPY INTO remains the recommended approach whenever files can be staged in storage first.

BCP API is exposed to three audiences: application developers (via SqlBulkCopy in C# or SQLServerBulkCopy in Java), script/runbook operators (via the bcp.exe command-line utility), and data-integration tool users (SSIS, Azure Data Factory, Informatica) whose connectors already use SQL bulk-copy semantics.
The capability is in preview and Microsoft is soliciting feedback via the Fabric Community Data Warehouse forum before general availability.

claims.text: Bulk Copy (BCP) API provides a client-side ingestion path for scenarios where data is produced in application code and must be written to warehouse tables directly, without a file-staging step, and it is in preview.

The recommended default ingestion approach in Fabric Data Warehouse remains server-side loading with COPY INTO whenever source files can be staged in storage first; BCP API addresses a different class of problem where staging isn't possible.

BCP API is recommended over issuing many row-by-row INSERT statements in client-side scenarios such as services receiving event batches, reading local files, or bulk-load connectors inside data-integration tools.
Application developers can call BCP API directly from client code using the SqlBulkCopy class in C# or the SQLServerBulkCopy class in Java to write in-memory data straight to a destination table.
The bcp.exe command-line utility exposes the same BCP API bulk-copy model for script-driven and runbook-based operational imports, run from a terminal rather than from application code.

Data-integration tools such as SSIS, Informatica, and Azure Data Factory can use the same client-side BCP API bulk-ingestion model transparently, because their SQL bulk-load connectors rely on BCP API semantics under the hood.
Sending data via bulk-copy semantics (batched writes) instead of many individual single-row INSERT statements is the stated mechanism by which BCP API improves ingestion throughput.
